title: Binary Tree Right Side View
directAnswer: Standing on the right of the tree, you see exactly one node per level — the rightmost one at each depth. Two clean ways: BFS by level and keep the last node dequeued in each level, or DFS visiting right-before-left and recording the first node seen at each new depth. Both are O(n) time; DFS is O(h) space.

remember.formula:
# DFS, right-first
def dfs(node, depth):
    if not node: return
    if depth == len(view): view.append(node.val)  # first at this depth = rightmost
    dfs(node.right, depth + 1)
    dfs(node.left,  depth + 1)
rules: The answer is **one value per level** — the rightmost node at each depth, NOT the right-edge/right-spine of the tree.
A left subtree node can be visible if the right subtree is **shorter** — don't just follow right children.
BFS: take the **last** node you dequeue in each level. DFS: visit **right before left** and record the first node at each new depth.
Track depth so you record **exactly one** value per level.
Empty tree → empty list; guard the null root.
whenToUse: You need one representative per level (rightmost, leftmost, max, min, average)
'What's visible from one side', 'last/first in each row' style questions
Any level-grouped problem where you collapse each level to a single value
Right-side / left-side view, largest value per row, bottom-up views
antiSignals: You need all nodes per level → full level-order traversal instead
The tree is a pure right spine and you mistakenly think that's always the answer → it isn't when left subtrees go deeper
You need the boundary/outline of the tree → that's the Boundary of Binary Tree problem, different logic
remember.takeaway: The right side view is the rightmost node of each level. Whether you BFS and grab the last per level or DFS right-first and grab the first per depth, the unifying idea is 'collapse each level to one representative'. The visible-from-shorter-left-subtree case is the trap that separates a real understanding from pattern-matching on right children.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you realize the answer is the rightmost node per level (not the right spine), and whether you can reduce a level-order traversal to one value per level — via BFS-last or DFS-right-first.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Just walking down the right children, which fails when a left subtree extends deeper than the right one and contributes the visible node for those lower levels.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Call out the 'left node visible when right subtree is shorter' case with a concrete example, then give the DFS right-first solution in O(h) space and mention BFS as the equally valid alternative.

problemStatement:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, imagine yourself standing on the ***right side*** of it. Return the values of the nodes you can see ordered from ***top to bottom***.

For each level of the tree, the visible node is the one furthest to the right at that depth.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 100]
understanding: For every depth, exactly one node is visible from the right: the rightmost one at that depth. The result lists those rightmost nodes from the top level down. Crucially, the visible node may come from a left subtree if the right subtree doesn't reach that depth.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is it the right spine of the tree or the rightmost node per level?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Rightmost per level. If the right subtree is shorter than the left, the deeper visible nodes come from the left subtree — so it's not simply the right edge.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Top-to-bottom order?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — index 0 is the root (the only level-0 node), then the rightmost of each successive level downward.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the tree be empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Return an empty list and guard the null root.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are values unique?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Not guaranteed, but it doesn't matter — we select by position (rightmost), not by value.

examples.explanation: Level 0: 1. Level 1: rightmost is 3. Level 2: 5 (under 2) and 4 (under 3); rightmost is 4.
Level 2 has only node 4 (left child of 2). The right subtree (3) has no children, so the left-subtree node 4 is the visible one.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Both BFS-last-per-level and DFS-right-first give the rightmost node per depth; DFS wins on space.

approaches.name: BFS — Last Node of Each Level
approaches.whenToMention: Natural first answer: 'right side view = the last node in each level of a level-order traversal'.
hints: If you traversed the tree level by level, which node in each level is the one you'd see from the right?
Run standard BFS with the queue-size snapshot. The last node you dequeue in a level is its rightmost.
During each level's loop, when the index reaches levelSize - 1 (or simply overwrite a variable each iteration), record that node's value.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Standard BFS visits each node once → O(n) time. The queue can hold a whole level → O(n) space in the worst case.
approaches.explanation:
This builds directly on level-order traversal. We process the tree one level at a time; the visible node for a level is simply the last one we touch in that level.

**Reusing the level-size snapshot.** As in level-order traversal, we read `levelSize = queue.size()` before draining a level so children don't leak in. Within the level loop we don't need the whole row — we just remember the most recent node, and after the loop the last one remembered is the rightmost. (Enqueueing left-then-right means the last dequeued is the furthest right.)

**Why the last node is the visible one.** Because we enqueue children left before right at every step, each level enters the queue in left-to-right order. Draining the level in FIFO order means the final dequeued node sits furthest right — exactly what an observer on the right sees.

**This handles the shorter-right-subtree case for free.** We never assume the visible node descends from a right child. If only a left-subtree node exists at some depth, it's still the last (and only) node dequeued for that level, so it's correctly recorded.
approaches.insight: Right side view is 'level-order traversal, but collapse each level to its last element'. That reframing makes the trap (left node visible when the right subtree is shorter) disappear, because BFS-by-level doesn't care which subtree a node came from.

dryRun.intro: BFS by level; record the last node dequeued in each level.

java.explanation: Snapshot the level boundary before enqueuing children (same as level-order traversal).
The last node dequeued in the level is its rightmost — that's what's visible.
Left before right means the last dequeued is furthest right.

python.explanation: Freeze the level size so children stay in the next round.
Record only the last node of each level.
Enqueue left then right; FIFO order makes the last popped the rightmost.

pitfalls: Recording the first node instead of the last (that would be a left-side view).
Re-reading queue size inside the loop, merging levels.

approaches.name: DFS Right-First — First Node Per Depth (Optimal Space)
approaches.whenToMention: The elegant answer. 'Visit right before left; the first node I reach at each new depth is the rightmost.'
hints: If you recurse into the right child before the left child, which node at each depth do you reach first?
Carry a depth argument. The first time you arrive at a given depth, that node is the rightmost for that level.
Compare depth to the size of your result list: if they're equal, you've reached a new depth for the first time — append this node, then recurse right then left.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each node is visited once → O(n). Only the recursion stack is extra, bounded by the tree height → O(h) space, better than BFS's O(width).
approaches.explanation:
Instead of materializing each level, we let recursion order do the selection. Visiting the right child first guarantees the first node we ever reach at a depth is the rightmost one.

**Why right-before-left works.** Pre-order DFS reaches a node before any of its descendants. If at each node we recurse into the right subtree first, then among all nodes at a given depth the one encountered earliest is the furthest right. So 'first node seen at depth d' equals 'rightmost node at depth d'.

**The 'new depth' test.** We keep `view` where `view[d]` is the rightmost node at depth d. When we descend to depth `d` and `len(view) == d`, it means we have not recorded depth `d` yet, so this node — the first arrival — is the rightmost. We append it. Every later node at depth `d` finds `len(view) > d` and is skipped.

**Why this nails the trap case.** Suppose the right subtree is shorter. At the deeper levels the right side has no nodes, so the first (and only) arrivals at those depths come from the left subtree — and the `len(view) == depth` test records them. We never assume the visible node is a right child.

**Space win.** DFS only keeps a root-to-leaf path on the stack, O(h), versus BFS holding a full level, O(width). For balanced trees the widest level is ~n/2, so DFS can be markedly leaner.
approaches.insight: Order of recursion is a selection mechanism. By choosing right-before-left, 'first seen at this depth' becomes 'rightmost at this depth' with no comparisons. Swap to left-before-right and the identical skeleton produces the left side view.

dryRun.intro: DFS right-first; record a node only when depth == len(view).

code.python:
# Definition for a binary tree node.
# class TreeNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.left = left
#         self.right = right
def rightSideView(self, root: 'TreeNode') -> list[int]:
    view: list[int] = []

    def dfs(node: 'TreeNode', depth: int) -> None:
        if node is None:
            return
        if depth == len(view):
            view.append(node.val)
        dfs(node.right, depth + 1)
        dfs(node.left, depth + 1)

    dfs(root, 0)
    return view

java.explanation: First arrival at this depth → because we go right-first, it's the rightmost node.
Right subtree BEFORE left — this ordering is what makes 'first seen' = 'rightmost'.
Left subtree still explored, so it can supply visible nodes where the right subtree is shorter.

python.explanation: We haven't recorded this depth yet, so this node is the rightmost for its level.
Visit right first so the rightmost node is reached first at each depth.
Left subtree still visited to cover deeper levels the right side doesn't reach.

diagrams.title: Why a left node can be visible
diagrams.caption: Right subtree of 1 (node 3) ends at depth 2 via node 4; node 5 under 2 is at the same depth but to its left, so 4 wins level 2.

edgeCases.behavior: Right subtree (3) is childless; at depth 2 only node 4 exists, and DFS right-first records it → [1,3,4].
Each level has one node from the left chain; every one is the rightmost-by-default → [1,2,3].
dfs returns immediately; view stays empty → [].

pitfalls: Recursing left before right — produces the LEFT side view.
Using a 'visited depth' set incorrectly; the len(view) == depth test is simpler and correct.
Assuming the answer is the right spine — fails when the left subtree is deeper.

commonMistakes: Returning the right spine (right children only) instead of the rightmost node per level.
DFS recursing left before right, which yields the left side view.
BFS recording the first node of each level rather than the last.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Following only right children
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Walking down node.right misses levels where the right subtree is shorter than the left. On [1,2,3,4] the right child of root (3) has no children, but node 4 (left child of 2) is visible at depth 2.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
node, view = root, []
while node:                 # only the right spine
    view.append(node.val)
    node = node.right

commonMistakesDetailed.title: DFS in the wrong child order
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you recurse left before right, the first node recorded at each depth is the leftmost, so you build the left side view instead of the right.

patternNote: Per-level extremum. Collapse each level of a tree to a single representative — rightmost, leftmost, max, or average. The DFS-order-as-selection trick (right-first → rightmost) and the BFS last-per-level trick both reduce to 'one value per depth'. Same family as Largest Value in Each Row and level averages.
